title: What education and CPD do Australian financial advisers need?
description: The qualifications, exam, professional year, CPD hours and Code of Ethics that apply to Australian relevant providers, including the 1 January 2026 deadline.
shortAnswer: Australian financial advisers who give personal advice to retail clients on relevant financial products (relevant providers) must hold an approved degree or equivalent qualification, pass the financial adviser exam, complete a professional year unless exempt, meet the Code of Ethics, and complete at least 40 hours of continuing professional development (CPD) each year. Existing advisers had until 1 January 2026 to meet the qualifications standard or rely on the experienced provider pathway.
keyTakeaways: The qualifications standard is in section 921B(2) of the Corporations Act, with approved degrees listed in a 2021 ministerial Determination.
The 1 January 2026 deadline for existing providers has passed. Those who had not met the standard lost relevant provider status and now need an approved degree and, usually, the professional year.

The experienced provider pathway needs 10 years (3,650 days) as a relevant provider between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2021, a clean disciplinary record at 31 December 2021, and a written declaration.
CPD is at least 40 hours a year (36 for approved part-timers), with at least 70% approved by the licensee and set minimums in four mandatory categories.
Licensees record qualifications and CPD failures on the Financial Advisers Register, and ASIC has used the register to identify advisers who had not met the standard.
appliesTo: Relevant providers: individuals authorised to give personal advice to retail clients on relevant financial products
Provisional relevant providers undertaking the professional year
AFS licensees that authorise relevant providers
Relevant providers who give tax (financial) advice services

sections.heading: What are the professional standards for financial advisers?

blocks.text: Relevant providers must meet five linked standards: an approved qualification, the financial adviser exam, the professional year (for new entrants), annual CPD, and the Financial Planners and Advisers Code of Ethics 2019. The standards have applied since 1 January 2019. They do not apply to people who only give general advice or advice on basic banking, general insurance or consumer credit insurance; those advisers remain under [RG 146](/regulations/asic-rg-146-training-requirements).

sections.heading: What happened at the 1 January 2026 qualifications deadline?

blocks.text: Existing providers had until 1 January 2026 to meet the qualifications standard, and those still authorised on that date without meeting it lost their relevant provider status by operation of law. ASIC's [qualifications standard page](https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/financial-services/financial-advice/professional-standards/qualifications-standard) sets out the three ways existing providers could meet it: an approved degree or equivalent, an existing provider pathway in Part 3 of the [Determination](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2021L01848/latest/text), or the experienced provider pathway.

Someone who lost status on 1 January 2026 cannot now use the Part 3 existing provider pathways. To be reauthorised they need an approved degree and the professional year, unless they are eligible for the experienced provider pathway, in which case a written declaration to their licensee meets both the qualifications and professional year standards. ASIC reported in 2026 that a review of the register found 132 existing providers with no qualifications marked as meeting the standard; after ASIC contacted their 82 licensees, 106 records were updated and 26 advisers had their authorisation ceased ([ASIC update](https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/news-items/asic-issues-update-on-compliance-with-the-financial-adviser-qualifications-standard)).

The [experienced provider pathway](https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/financial-services/financial-advice/professional-standards/accessing-the-experienced-provider-pathway) (INFO 281) requires at least 10 years (3,650 days, consecutive or not) as a relevant provider between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2021, and a clean disciplinary record as at 31 December 2021.

sections.heading: What do new entrants need before giving unsupervised advice?

blocks.text: A new entrant must complete an approved degree, pass the exam, complete the professional year, be authorised by a licensee and be registered with ASIC before giving unsupervised personal advice. ASIC's [professional year checklist](https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/financial-services/financial-advice/professional-standards/professional-year) describes the sequence:

items: Agree a professional year plan with a supervisor and the responsible licensee.
Complete quarters 1 and 2, keeping a logbook of work activities and structured training, and obtain a completion certificate for each quarter.
Before quarter 3, meet the qualifications standard, pass the exam and be authorised to give personal advice. The licensee appoints the person to the register as a provisional relevant provider.
Complete quarter 3, including identifying and resolving at least two ethical dilemmas, and quarter 4.
Complete at least 100 hours of structured training and 1,500 hours of work activities over a minimum one-year period, then move to relevant provider status and registration.

blocks.text: The professional year is a structured workplace program, so it suits a [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) that defines the observable tasks each quarter should evidence.

sections.heading: How many CPD hours do financial advisers need?

blocks.text: Relevant providers must complete at least 40 hours of CPD each CPD year, reduced to 36 hours if they work part time for the whole year and have their licensee's prior written consent. ASIC's [CPD page](https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/financial-services/financial-advice/professional-standards/continuing-professional-development-cpd) sets out the structure under the [CPD Determination](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2018L01817/latest/text):

blocks.text: At least 70% of the applicable minimum hours must be qualifying CPD activities approved by the authorising licensee, and the balance up to 40 hours must also be qualifying CPD. The relevant provider or licensee must keep complete and accurate CPD records and provide them to the licensee on request, and licensees must update the register if an adviser fails to meet the annual requirement. Provisional relevant providers are not subject to the CPD standard but complete structured training in their professional year.

The authorising licensee decides whether an adviser's qualifications meet the standard, approves most CPD, keeps the register accurate, and remains responsible for advice quality. ASIC says individuals and licensees are responsible for deciding whether a degree meets the standard, and that ASIC does not assess individual qualifications. Licensees must update the register within 30 business days after a relevant provider completes relevant qualifications and training.

A defensible licensee file for each adviser typically holds: the qualification and the Determination item it meets (or the experienced provider declaration and ASIC notification), exam evidence, professional year certificates where relevant, a CPD plan with activities tagged to categories, approval records for qualifying activities, and a year end reconciliation. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers how to structure this.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry can represent the CPD categories, the Code of Ethics standards and a licensee's own advice obligations as one framework, so each CPD activity is tagged to what it covers and each adviser's gaps are visible before the year ends. The same structure supports professional year plans with defined assessment points each quarter.

faqs.q: Can an adviser who missed the 1 January 2026 deadline still use the experienced provider pathway?
faqs.a: Yes, if they are eligible. ASIC says an existing provider who meets the experienced provider criteria but did not make the declaration before 1 January 2026 can meet the qualifications and professional year standards by making the written declaration to their licensee. They then need reauthorisation and registration.

faqs.q: Does the exam count towards the qualifications standard?
faqs.a: No. ASIC has warned licensees to check that the financial adviser exam has not been incorrectly marked on the register as going toward the qualifications standard, and that marking only an ethics course is insufficient.

The authorising AFS licensee approves qualifying CPD activities. At least 70% of the applicable minimum hours must be activities the licensee has approved. The Minister does not approve individual CPD activities.

faqs.q: Do general advice staff need to meet these standards?
faqs.a: No. The professional standards apply to relevant providers, who give personal advice to retail clients on relevant financial products. Staff who only give general advice, or personal advice on basic banking, general insurance or consumer credit insurance, are covered by RG 146.
